SS.L4.HIS.T01.title: Local history
SS.L4.HIS.T01.description: Finding out about the past of a local area through pictures, writing, stories, interviews and objects.
SS.L4.HIS.T01.recovery_strategy: We learn about the past through clues — pictures, writing, stories, interviews and objects. Each clue gives a different kind of information.

questions.question: What does 'history' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the word history mean?
options: The study of what happened in the past
A school subject only about kings
questions.expected: The study of what happened in the past
questions.memo: History is the study of the past — what people did, what changed, what stayed the same. Not just kings — ordinary people too.

questions.question: Which is a way to find out about the past?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a way to find out about the past?
options: A new TV show made today
questions.expected: Old photographs of the area
questions.memo: Old photos are a window into the past — clothes, buildings, transport all show how life was different.

questions.question: True or false: Talking to an elder is a good way to learn local history.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: talking to an elder is a good way to learn about your local history.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Elders carry stories of how things were. An interview with a grandparent is real history — it just isn't written down.

questions.question: An OBJECT from the past — like an old coin or tool — is a clue about:
questions.ruby_prompt: An old coin or old tool found in a place — what kind of clue is it?
options: How people lived in the past
questions.expected: How people lived in the past
questions.memo: Objects tell us about daily life — what people used, made and valued. An old farming tool says people farmed; an old coin says they traded.

questions.question: Sipho wants to find out what his town looked like 50 years ago. What is the BEST first step?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho wants to know what his town looked like 50 years ago. What's a good first step?
options: Look at old photographs of the town and talk to people who lived there
questions.expected: Look at old photographs of the town and talk to people who lived there
questions.memo: Photographs + interviews = a strong start. Photos show what; people fill in the story behind what.

questions.question: Which is an example of WRITING that tells us about the past?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is an example of writing that tells us about the past?
options: An old letter, an old newspaper or an old book
questions.expected: An old letter, an old newspaper or an old book
questions.memo: Writing from the past — letters, diaries, newspapers, books — gives us the words people used and the things they thought were worth recording.

questions.question: What is an 'interview' in history?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean to do an interview when you're learning history?
options: Asking someone questions to learn from their experience
questions.expected: Asking someone questions to learn from their experience
questions.memo: An interview is a guided conversation. You ask questions; they share what they remember. It's one of the simplest history tools there is.

questions.question: True or false: All information about the past must come from books.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the only way to learn about the past is from books.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Stories, photos, objects, songs, buildings, interviews — all of these are also valid ways to learn the past.

questions.question: Why is it important to learn about the LOCAL history of your area?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does it matter to learn about the history of your own local area?
options: It helps you understand the place you live in and the people before you
questions.expected: It helps you understand the place you live in and the people before you
questions.memo: Local history is YOUR history. It explains why the streets, names, buildings and families around you are the way they are.

questions.question: Karabo found an old map of her village from 1960. What is this map?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo finds an old map of her village from 1960. What kind of clue about the past is this?
options: A picture-clue showing how the village was arranged long ago
questions.expected: A picture-clue showing how the village was arranged long ago
questions.memo: An old map is a picture-clue. Compare it to today's map and you can see what changed — new roads, new buildings, vanished features.

questions.question: Put these in order — a simple plan to research your local history.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — a simple plan for researching local history.
options: Choose a question about your area
Look for clues (photos, books, objects, people)
questions.expected: Choose a question about your area,Look for clues (photos, books, objects, people),Write down what you find,Share your findings
questions.memo: Question → clues → notes → share. Every historian does this, no matter how big or small the project.

questions.question: True or false: Different people can remember the same event in different ways.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: two different people might remember the same event in different ways.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. That's why historians look at MANY sources. One person's memory is one view; together they give a fuller picture.

questions.question: Which is NOT a way to learn local history?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is NOT really a way to learn local history?
options: Making up a story with no clues
questions.expected: Making up a story with no clues
questions.memo: History needs CLUES, not invention. Making things up is fiction, not history. Real history is grounded in what we can find.

questions.question: Mpho's grandfather tells a story about how the river near his village used to flood every year. This is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho's grandfather tells a story about how the river used to flood every year. What kind of clue is this?
options: An oral story — a real source of local history
questions.expected: An oral story — a real source of local history
questions.memo: Oral stories — passed down by speaking — are one of the oldest forms of history. They carry knowledge that may not be in any book.

questions.question: Which question would help you start a local history project?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which question would be a good START to a local history project?
options: 'What was my street like 50 years ago?'
questions.expected: 'What was my street like 50 years ago?'
questions.memo: A good history question is SPECIFIC and looks BACKWARDS in time. 'What was X like in Y year' gives you something to research.

questions.question: True or false: An old building is also a clue about the past.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: an old building can be a clue about the past.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Old buildings tell us about what people built with, what they needed (church, school, station) and how the area grew.

questions.question: Why should we use MORE than one source when learning local history?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it better to use more than one source when you learn local history?
options: Different sources fill in different parts and help us check what's true
questions.expected: Different sources fill in different parts and help us check what's true
questions.memo: One source = one view. Many sources = a fuller, more reliable picture. Historians always cross-check.

questions.question: Lerato wants to interview an elder. Which question is BEST?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato is going to interview an elder. Which question is the best one to ask?
options: 'What was the school like when you were a child?'
questions.expected: 'What was the school like when you were a child?'
questions.memo: Good interview questions are open ('what was it like'), polite, and focused on the past. They invite stories, not yes/no answers.

questions.question: Tell me ONE thing in your local area you'd like to know the history of.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing in your local area you'd like to know the history of — a building, a place name, a road, anything.
questions.expected: Why my street has its name
questions.memo: Good answers: any local feature — a building, a school, a road name, an old shop, a tree, a hill. Curiosity about your own place is the start of real history.

questions.question: What is the BEST description of a 'historian'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best description of a historian?
options: A person who studies clues from the past to understand what happened
A person who only reads new books
A person who watches TV all day
questions.expected: A person who studies clues from the past to understand what happened
questions.memo: A historian is a careful detective of the past. They gather clues, check sources, and put the story together — like you doing your local project.

SS.L4.HIS.T02.title: Learning from leaders
SS.L4.HIS.T02.description: Qualities of good leaders, using Nelson Mandela and Mahatma Gandhi as examples.
SS.L4.HIS.T02.recovery_strategy: Anchor leadership to actions. Mandela and Gandhi served others, listened, had courage, and were willing to suffer for their beliefs. That's what made them great — not fame.

questions.question: Who was Nelson Mandela?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Nelson Mandela?
options: A South African leader who fought against apartheid and became the first democratic president
questions.expected: A South African leader who fought against apartheid and became the first democratic president
questions.memo: Nelson Mandela led the fight against apartheid, spent 27 years in prison for his beliefs, and became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994.

questions.question: Who was Mahatma Gandhi?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who was Mahatma Gandhi?
options: An Indian leader who fought injustice peacefully
questions.expected: An Indian leader who fought injustice peacefully
questions.memo: Gandhi led India to independence using peaceful protest, not violence. He spent many years in South Africa first, where he developed his ideas about non-violent resistance.

questions.question: Which is a quality of a GOOD leader?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a quality of a good leader?
options: Listens to people and works for the good of others
questions.expected: Listens to people and works for the good of others
questions.memo: A real leader serves. Listening + working for others is the heart of good leadership — that's what made Mandela and Gandhi great.

questions.question: True or false: A good leader must have COURAGE.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: a good leader needs to have courage.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Courage means doing what's right even when it's hard or scary. Both Mandela and Gandhi showed courage many times.

questions.question: Mandela was in PRISON for how many years for fighting apartheid?
questions.ruby_prompt: How many years did Nelson Mandela spend in prison for fighting apartheid?
questions.expected: 27 years
questions.memo: Mandela was imprisoned for 27 years. He was released in 1990. Four years later he was elected president — the same country that jailed him now chose him to lead it.

questions.question: True or false: Gandhi believed in fighting with WEAPONS.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Gandhi believed in fighting with weapons.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Gandhi believed in NON-VIOLENT resistance — peaceful protest, not weapons. He believed violence only created more violence.

questions.question: Which is the BEST example of 'working as a team'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the best example of a leader working as a team?
options: Asking advisors for ideas and listening before deciding
Making all decisions alone and ignoring everyone
questions.expected: Asking advisors for ideas and listening before deciding
questions.memo: Good leaders gather wise people around them. No one person knows everything. A team multiplies your wisdom.

questions.question: What does 'sacrifice' mean for a leader?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the word sacrifice mean when we talk about a leader?
options: Giving up something important for the good of others
questions.expected: Giving up something important for the good of others
questions.memo: Sacrifice = giving up time, safety, comfort or freedom for a bigger cause. Mandela sacrificed his freedom; Gandhi sacrificed his comfort and safety.

questions.question: Mandela said leaders should be like a SHEPHERD. What did he mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: Mandela said a leader should be like a shepherd. What did he mean by that?
options: Walk behind the people, letting the most clever go first, and gently keep everyone together
questions.expected: Walk behind the people, letting the most clever go first, and gently keep everyone together
questions.memo: Mandela said a great leader walks behind — letting others lead the way and gently guiding from the back. Service over ego.

questions.question: True or false: Good leaders are ALWAYS popular.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: a good leader is always popular with everyone.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Doing the right thing often upsets people. Mandela was hated by some for refusing apartheid; Gandhi was hated for his ideas. Real leadership isn't a popularity contest.

questions.question: True or false: Good leaders are PERFECT.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: good leaders are perfect.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. No leader is perfect. Mandela made mistakes; Gandhi made mistakes. What matters is how they kept trying and kept doing what they believed was right.

questions.question: How can ORDINARY people follow the example of leaders like Mandela?
questions.ruby_prompt: How can ordinary people follow the example of great leaders like Mandela?
options: Be kind, fair and brave in everyday choices
Only follow them if they are alive
questions.expected: Be kind, fair and brave in everyday choices
questions.memo: You don't need to lead a country to lead. Be kind in the classroom; stand up for someone being bullied; listen to others. Big leadership = many small acts.

questions.question: Which act shows Gandhi's 'wholehearted commitment to his beliefs'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these shows Gandhi's wholehearted commitment to his beliefs?
options: He went to prison many times rather than stop protesting unjust laws
He gave up after the first arrest
He never spoke about his beliefs
He changed his mind whenever criticised
questions.expected: He went to prison many times rather than stop protesting unjust laws
questions.memo: Gandhi was arrested over and over. He never stopped — that's wholehearted commitment. Real beliefs survive hardship.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a quality of a good leader?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is NOT a quality of a good leader?
options: Refusing to listen to anyone else
questions.expected: Refusing to listen to anyone else
questions.memo: A leader who won't listen is a tyrant, not a leader. Listening is the FIRST skill of leadership.

questions.question: Why did Mandela choose forgiveness AFTER prison?
questions.ruby_prompt: After 27 years in prison, why did Mandela choose forgiveness instead of revenge?
options: He believed revenge would keep South Africa divided; forgiveness could rebuild it
questions.expected: He believed revenge would keep South Africa divided; forgiveness could rebuild it
questions.memo: Mandela's choice to forgive — even his jailers — is one of the great acts of leadership in human history. He chose the country over himself.

questions.question: Put these in order — a child practising leadership at school.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — a child practising good leadership at school.
options: Notice someone is being treated unfairly
Stay calm and think about what's right
Speak up kindly or ask a teacher for help
Follow through and stand with the person
questions.expected: Notice someone is being treated unfairly,Stay calm and think about what's right,Speak up kindly or ask a teacher for help,Follow through and stand with the person
questions.memo: Notice → think → speak → stand. Big leaders started with small acts like this when they were children.

questions.question: Tell me one quality you ADMIRE about Mandela or Gandhi.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one quality you admire about Mandela or Gandhi.
questions.expected: I admire that Mandela forgave the people who put him in prison
questions.memo: Good answers: courage, kindness, patience, fairness, forgiveness, commitment, willingness to suffer for others. Any of these are real.

questions.question: Which is a TRUE statement about leadership?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is true about leadership?
options: Leadership is shown in actions, not in titles
You must be rich to be a leader
questions.expected: Leadership is shown in actions, not in titles
questions.memo: Leadership = what you DO. A child who stands up for a friend is leading. A president who lies is not leading. Title doesn't make the leader.

questions.question: Both Mandela and Gandhi were willing to suffer for their cause. This is called:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mandela and Gandhi were both willing to suffer for what they believed in. What's a word for this?
questions.expected: Sacrifice
questions.memo: Sacrifice — giving up something valuable for a bigger cause. The mark of a great leader.

questions.question: What was Gandhi doing in SOUTH AFRICA before he became famous in India?
questions.ruby_prompt: Before Gandhi became famous in India, what was he doing in South Africa?
options: He was a lawyer who began fighting against laws that treated Indian people unfairly
He had never been to South Africa
questions.expected: He was a lawyer who began fighting against laws that treated Indian people unfairly
questions.memo: Gandhi spent 21 years in South Africa as a lawyer. The injustice he saw — and faced — here shaped the ideas he later used to free India.

SS.L4.HIS.T03.title: Transport through time
SS.L4.HIS.T03.description: How transport on land, water and in the air has changed over time.
SS.L4.HIS.T03.recovery_strategy: Transport changed from slow to fast, from animal-power to engine-power. Each new invention solved a problem: how to go further, faster, or carry more.

questions.question: Before machines, what did people use to travel on land?
questions.ruby_prompt: Before there were machines, what did people use to travel on land?
options: Animals like horses, donkeys and oxen
questions.expected: Animals like horses, donkeys and oxen
questions.memo: For thousands of years, animals carried us and our things. Horses pulled carts; oxen pulled wagons; donkeys carried loads.

questions.question: Which is the OLDEST form of transport on water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the oldest form of transport on water?
questions.expected: Rafts and canoes
questions.memo: Rafts and canoes were the first water transport — simple wood, powered by paddles or the current. Humans have used them for thousands of years.

questions.question: Who invented the first powered aeroplane?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who invented the first powered aeroplane?
questions.expected: The Wright brothers
questions.memo: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew the first powered aeroplane in 1903 in the United States. Their flight lasted only 12 seconds — and changed the world.

questions.question: The STEAM ENGINE was powered by:
questions.ruby_prompt: What powered the steam engine?
options: Steam from boiling water (using coal or wood as fuel)
questions.expected: Steam from boiling water (using coal or wood as fuel)
questions.memo: Steam engines boiled water with fire (usually from coal). The steam pushed pistons that turned wheels. This powered the first trains.

questions.question: Which came FIRST?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which came first?
questions.expected: The horse-drawn cart
questions.memo: Carts pulled by animals came thousands of years before any engine. Cars, planes and rockets are all from the last 200 years.

questions.question: True or false: The bicycle was invented BEFORE the motor car.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the bicycle was invented before the motor car.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Bicycles were around by the early 1800s; the motor car only came in the late 1800s. The bicycle is still one of the smartest inventions ever.

questions.question: Put these in the right order — OLDEST to NEWEST.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order from oldest to newest.
questions.expected: Horse and wagon,Steam train,Motor car,Aeroplane
questions.memo: Wagons (ancient) → trains (1800s) → cars (late 1800s) → planes (early 1900s). Each century brought faster transport.

questions.question: What kind of ship is a 'CARAVEL'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What kind of ship is a caravel?
options: A small sailing ship used by early European explorers
questions.expected: A small sailing ship used by early European explorers
questions.memo: Caravels were small, fast sailing ships. Portuguese explorers like Dias used caravels to sail down the coast of Africa over 500 years ago.

questions.question: What was the MAIN advantage of trains over horse-drawn wagons?
questions.ruby_prompt: What was the main advantage of trains compared to horse-drawn wagons?
options: Trains carry many more people and goods, much faster, over long distances
questions.expected: Trains carry many more people and goods, much faster, over long distances
questions.memo: Trains transformed travel — what took a wagon weeks took a train days, with much bigger loads. They changed how countries worked.

questions.question: Why is air pollution from cars a PROBLEM in big cities?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is exhaust fume air pollution from cars a problem in big cities?
options: It makes the air unhealthy to breathe and harms people's health
questions.expected: It makes the air unhealthy to breathe and harms people's health
questions.memo: Car exhaust adds harmful gases to the air. In big cities with lots of cars, this makes breathing harder and can damage lungs and the planet.

questions.question: Modern aeroplanes are powered by:
questions.ruby_prompt: What powers modern aeroplanes?
questions.expected: Jet engines that burn fuel
questions.memo: Jet engines suck in air, burn fuel inside, and shoot the hot gas out the back to push the plane forward. Much faster than older propeller engines.

questions.question: True or false: The first sailing ships had no engines.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the first sailing ships had no engines.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Sailing ships use the WIND as their power. Sailors had to read the weather and use sails cleverly to catch the wind.

questions.question: A 'STEAMSHIP' uses what to move?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does a steamship move?
options: A steam engine that turns paddle wheels or propellers
questions.expected: A steam engine that turns paddle wheels or propellers
questions.memo: Steamships could travel without depending on wind — a huge change. Ships could now plan routes and arrive on time.

questions.question: Which modern transport is the FASTEST way to travel between continents?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the fastest way to travel between continents today?
questions.expected: Aeroplane
questions.memo: A flight that takes 10 hours by plane would take weeks by ship. Air travel made the world feel small.

questions.question: Why might someone choose a BICYCLE over a car?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might someone choose a bicycle instead of a car?
options: No fuel needed, no air pollution, good exercise, cheap to keep
questions.expected: No fuel needed, no air pollution, good exercise, cheap to keep
questions.memo: Bicycles are clean, cheap, healthy and quiet. In many cities people are going back to bicycles for short trips.

questions.question: Lerato's great-grandmother used to walk 5km to school. Why might that have been normal back then?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's great-grandmother used to walk 5km to school every day. Why was that normal back then?
options: Cars and buses were rare or unavailable in many areas
questions.expected: Cars and buses were rare or unavailable in many areas
questions.memo: For most of history, walking was the main way to get around. Cars and buses are very recent — especially in rural South African areas.

questions.question: Which transport carries the MOST goods in one trip?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which transport can carry the most goods in one trip?
questions.expected: A large ship
questions.memo: Modern container ships can carry thousands of tonnes of goods — far more than any plane, train or truck. Most world trade still moves by sea.

questions.question: Tell me one way transport has CHANGED your family's life.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one way transport has changed life for your family — your parents or grandparents.
questions.expected: My grandparents used to walk far to fetch water but now there are taps
questions.memo: Good answers: cars made trips faster; taxis let people travel for work; trains carry goods to shops; planes mean family far away can visit. All real changes.

questions.question: Why do most South African towns have a TRAIN STATION?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do most South African towns have a train station?
options: Trains have been an important way to move people and goods across the country
questions.expected: Trains have been an important way to move people and goods across the country
questions.memo: South Africa built a huge rail network in the 1800s to move people, gold and goods. Many towns grew up AROUND their train station.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about transport history?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which statement about transport history is true?
options: Each new transport invention solved a problem the older one had
All transport was invented at the same time
questions.expected: Each new transport invention solved a problem the older one had
questions.memo: Wagons were slow → trains. Trains can't fly → planes. Planes are expensive → ships still move heavy goods. Every invention answers a problem.

SS.L4.HIS.T04.title: Communication through time
SS.L4.HIS.T04.description: How communication has changed over time — from songs, symbols and art to postal systems, radio, telephone, TV, computers and cell phones.
SS.L4.HIS.T04.recovery_strategy: Communication is sharing a message. Long ago people used songs, symbols and art; today we use phones and the internet. The goal is the same — the tools got faster.

questions.question: What does 'communication' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the word communication mean?
options: Sharing information or a message with someone
questions.expected: Sharing information or a message with someone
questions.memo: Communication is any way of getting a message from one person to another — speaking, writing, drawing, even waving.

questions.question: Which is one of the OLDEST forms of human communication?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is one of the oldest forms of human communication?
questions.expected: Spoken language, songs and art
questions.memo: Speaking, singing and drawing pictures have been around as long as humans. The San people in Southern Africa used all three thousands of years ago.

questions.question: The San hunter-gatherers communicated through:
questions.ruby_prompt: How did the San hunter-gatherers communicate?
options: Language, stories, songs, dance and rock art
questions.expected: Language, stories, songs, dance and rock art
questions.memo: The San used spoken language, told stories, sang, danced and painted on rocks. Their rock art still teaches us about them today.

questions.question: What is a 'postal system'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a postal system?
options: A network for sending letters and parcels from place to place
questions.expected: A network for sending letters and parcels from place to place
questions.memo: Postal systems collect, sort and deliver letters and parcels. Before phones and email, they were the main way to send a message far away.

questions.question: Who invented the TELEPHONE?
questions.ruby_prompt: Who invented the telephone?
questions.expected: Alexander Graham Bell
questions.memo: Alexander Graham Bell made the first telephone call in 1876. For the first time, two people could speak across long distances.

questions.question: What does a RADIO do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a radio do?
options: Receives sound (like music and news) sent through invisible waves in the air
questions.expected: Receives sound (like music and news) sent through invisible waves in the air
questions.memo: Radio waves travel through the air. A radio set picks them up and turns them into sound. One radio station can reach millions of people at once.

questions.question: Put these in order — OLDEST to NEWEST.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order from oldest to newest.
questions.expected: Letter sent by post,Telephone call,Radio broadcast,Cell phone text message
questions.memo: Letters (very old) → telephone (1876) → radio (early 1900s) → SMS (1990s). Each step made messages faster and reached more people.

questions.question: True or false: The TELEGRAPH used electric signals to send messages along wires.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: the telegraph used electric signals to send messages along wires.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. The telegraph sent quick electric pulses along wires — using a code like Morse code. It was the first way to send messages almost instantly across long distances.

questions.question: What did the EARLY TYPEWRITER do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What did an early typewriter do?
options: Print letters onto paper when keys were pressed (before electricity)
questions.expected: Print letters onto paper when keys were pressed (before electricity)
questions.memo: Early typewriters were mechanical — no power needed. They let people produce clean, readable documents long before computers.

questions.question: What does a CAMERA do?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a camera do?
options: Captures an image of what is in front of it
questions.expected: Captures an image of what is in front of it
questions.memo: The camera changed history — it gave us a way to share what something LOOKED LIKE, exactly. Before that, only drawings and descriptions existed.

questions.question: True or false: TELEVISION combines pictures AND sound.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: television combines moving pictures and sound.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. TV is radio + moving pictures. It brought news, sport and stories into people's homes — a huge change in how families spent evenings.

questions.question: What is the INTERNET?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the internet?
options: A huge global network connecting computers and phones so they can share information
A new type of TV channel
questions.expected: A huge global network connecting computers and phones so they can share information
questions.memo: The internet connects billions of devices. It lets you share information with someone across the world in seconds — something no earlier tool could do.

questions.question: Why was the CELL PHONE such a big change?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why was the cell phone such a big change in communication?
options: People could call from almost anywhere, not just from a wired phone at home
Cell phones don't really do anything
questions.expected: People could call from almost anywhere, not just from a wired phone at home
questions.memo: Before cell phones, you had to find a wired phone (at home, at work, at a phone booth) to call anyone. Cell phones put a phone in everyone's pocket.

questions.question: Sipho's grandmother says, 'In my day we waited two weeks for a letter to arrive.' What does this show?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's grandmother says 'In my day we waited two weeks for a letter to arrive.' What does this tell us?
options: Communication was much SLOWER before today's phones and internet
questions.expected: Communication was much SLOWER before today's phones and internet
questions.memo: A letter going by post and ship could take weeks. Today an email crosses the same distance in seconds. The change in our lifetimes is enormous.

questions.question: Why are PICTURES used in communication?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do people use pictures to communicate?
options: Pictures share ideas quickly, even when people don't share a language
questions.expected: Pictures share ideas quickly, even when people don't share a language
questions.memo: A road sign with no words still tells you 'stop' or 'one way'. Pictures cross languages — that's why rock art still communicates with us thousands of years later.

questions.question: True or false: All forms of communication ever invented are now useless.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: all the old forms of communication are now useless.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. We still talk face to face, sing, dance, draw, write letters, use radio. New tools ADD options — they don't always replace the old ones.

questions.question: Which is a DOWNSIDE of cell phones and internet?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a downside of cell phones and internet?
options: People can spend too much time looking at screens and less time with each other
questions.expected: People can spend too much time looking at screens and less time with each other
questions.memo: Every new tool brings problems too. Phones connect us with people far away, but can pull us away from the people right in front of us.

questions.question: Karabo wants to invite her cousin to her birthday next month. Which is the FASTEST way?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo wants to invite her cousin in another town to her birthday next month. What's the fastest way to invite her today?
options: A phone call or text message
questions.expected: A phone call or text message
questions.memo: Today the message arrives in seconds. A letter could take a week. A telegram isn't really used any more. The change in speed is part of why life feels faster now.

questions.question: Tell me one way YOU communicate that your great-grandparent didn't have.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one way you communicate that your great-grandparent didn't have when they were your age.
questions.expected: I can video-call my friend on a cell phone
questions.memo: Good answers: cell phone, SMS, video call, email, social media, voice notes, online chat. Any of these are real and recent.

questions.question: Which statement about communication history is BEST?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which statement about the history of communication is best?
options: Each new invention let people share messages faster and further than before
Modern tools made the world smaller and louder
questions.expected: Each new invention let people share messages faster and further than before
questions.memo: From rock art (one cave) to internet (the whole world), each step extended REACH and SPEED. Same goal — share a message — bigger results.

SS.L4.GEO.T01.title: Places where people live (settlements)
SS.L4.GEO.T01.description: Farms, villages, towns and cities; buildings and their uses; landmarks; people's basic needs.
SS.L4.GEO.T01.recovery_strategy: Settlements are places where people live. Farms are smallest and most spread out; cities are biggest and have the most kinds of work. Landmarks help us find our way.

questions.question: What is a 'settlement'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a settlement?
questions.expected: A place where people live
questions.memo: A settlement is any place where people have set up homes — from a single farm to a huge city.

questions.question: Which is the BIGGEST kind of settlement?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is the biggest kind of settlement?
questions.expected: A city
questions.memo: From smallest to biggest: farm → village → town → city. Cities have thousands or millions of people and many kinds of work.

questions.question: Which is the SMALLEST kind of settlement?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the smallest kind of settlement?
questions.expected: A farm
questions.memo: A single farm is usually just one or two families. Most farms in South Africa are spread out, not crowded together.

questions.question: What is a 'landmark'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a landmark?
options: Something easy to see and recognise that helps people find their way
questions.expected: Something easy to see and recognise that helps people find their way
questions.memo: A landmark can be natural (a big tree, a hill) or built (a church, a tall building). It's a 'use this to know where you are' marker.

questions.question: Put these settlements in order — SMALLEST to BIGGEST.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order from smallest to biggest settlement.
questions.expected: Farm,Village,Town,City
questions.memo: Farm → village → town → city. Each level has MORE people and MORE kinds of buildings and jobs.

questions.question: Which building is for HEALTH care?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which building is for health care?
questions.expected: A clinic or hospital
questions.memo: Clinics handle everyday health needs; hospitals handle serious ones. Both are health buildings.

questions.question: Which is a NATURAL landmark?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a natural landmark?
questions.expected: A mountain
questions.memo: Natural landmarks (mountains, rivers, big trees) were made by nature. Human-made landmarks (bridges, towers) were built by people.

questions.question: Which is a HUMAN-MADE landmark?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a human-made landmark?
questions.expected: A church tower
questions.memo: Human-made = built by people. A church tower, a tall building, a bridge — these are all human-made landmarks.

questions.question: What do ALL people need to live?
questions.ruby_prompt: What do all people need to live?
options: Water, food, shelter, health care and energy
questions.expected: Water, food, shelter, health care and energy
questions.memo: Every human everywhere needs the basics: water to drink, food to eat, shelter from weather, health care when sick, energy for cooking and light.

questions.question: True or false: A village has FEWER people than a town.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: a village has fewer people than a town.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Villages are small — often a few hundred people. Towns are bigger and have more shops, schools and services.

questions.question: Sipho needs to tell his friend how to walk to his house. Which is BEST?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho needs to explain how to walk to his house. Which way of explaining is best?
options: 'Walk straight, turn right at the big tree, then left past the school'
questions.expected: 'Walk straight, turn right at the big tree, then left past the school'
questions.memo: Good directions use LANDMARKS (the big tree, the school) and DIRECTIONS (left, right, straight). That's how people find places.

questions.question: Which building is for WORSHIP?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which building is for worship?
options: A church, mosque, temple or synagogue
questions.expected: A church, mosque, temple or synagogue
questions.memo: Places of worship are where people pray and gather for their religion. South Africa has many — churches, mosques, temples, synagogues.

questions.question: Which is a TERTIARY (service) job?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a service job (helping people directly)?
options: A worker in a coal mine
questions.expected: A teacher in a school
questions.memo: Service jobs help people directly — teachers, doctors, taxi drivers, shop workers. Farming and mining are different (they get things from nature).

questions.question: Why are most FACTORIES found in towns and cities, not on farms?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why are most factories found in towns and cities, not on farms?
options: Towns and cities have more workers, transport and customers nearby
questions.expected: Towns and cities have more workers, transport and customers nearby
questions.memo: Factories need lots of workers and a way to send goods out. Cities provide both. Farms are spread out and far from buyers.

questions.question: Which describes a FOOTPATH?
questions.ruby_prompt: What describes a footpath?
options: A narrow path made for people walking, not for cars
questions.expected: A narrow path made for people walking, not for cars
questions.memo: Footpaths are walking paths — between houses, through fields, up hills. Many South African villages have more footpaths than roads.

questions.question: True or false: A FARM is usually MORE crowded with buildings than a city.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: a farm is usually more crowded with buildings than a city.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. Cities are very crowded — lots of buildings close together. Farms have open land between the buildings.

questions.question: Tell me ONE landmark in your area that helps people find their way.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one landmark in your area that helps people find their way.
questions.expected: The big church tower near my house
questions.memo: Good answers: a tall building, a clock tower, a church or mosque, a big tree, a hill, a sports stadium, a bridge, a market. All real.

questions.question: How do people in a city usually meet their FOOD need?
questions.ruby_prompt: How do most people in a city get their food?
options: They buy it from shops and supermarkets
They grow it on small farms inside the city
questions.expected: They buy it from shops and supermarkets
questions.memo: City people mostly buy food. The food was grown on farms, brought to factories or markets, then sold in shops. Farms feed cities.

questions.question: Why might someone MOVE from a farm to a city?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might a person move from a farm to a city?
options: More jobs, more schools, more services in cities
questions.expected: More jobs, more schools, more services in cities
questions.memo: Cities pull people in — more job choices, bigger schools, hospitals, shops. This is happening all over South Africa and the world.

questions.question: Which is the BEST description of a TOWN?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is the best description of a town?
options: A settlement bigger than a village but smaller than a city, with shops, schools and services
questions.expected: A settlement bigger than a village but smaller than a city, with shops, schools and services
questions.memo: Towns are in the middle: more than a village (which is mostly homes) but less than a city. Towns have shops, a clinic, schools — but not the scale of a city.

SS.L4.GEO.T03.title: Food and farming in South Africa
SS.L4.GEO.T03.description: Where food comes from; subsistence vs commercial farming; crop and stock farming in SA; unprocessed and processed foods.
SS.L4.GEO.T03.recovery_strategy: Food comes from plants (crops) or animals (stock). Subsistence farming feeds the family; commercial farming sells to others. Processed food has been changed from its raw form.

questions.question: Where does our food come from?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where does our food come from?
questions.expected: From plants and animals
questions.memo: All food starts with plants (crops) or animals (meat, milk, eggs). Shops and factories handle food — but they don't make it from scratch.

questions.question: What is 'crop farming'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is crop farming?
options: Growing plants like maize, wheat and fruit
questions.expected: Growing plants like maize, wheat and fruit
questions.memo: Crops are plants people grow to eat or sell — maize, wheat, fruit, vegetables. Crop farming = growing plants on purpose.

questions.question: What is 'stock farming'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is stock farming?
options: Raising animals like cattle, sheep, goats and chickens
questions.expected: Raising animals like cattle, sheep, goats and chickens
questions.memo: Stock = farm animals. Stock farming includes large stock (cattle), small stock (sheep, goats) and poultry (chickens).

questions.question: What is 'SUBSISTENCE farming'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does subsistence farming mean?
options: Farming to feed your own family, not to sell
Farming to make a lot of money
questions.expected: Farming to feed your own family, not to sell
questions.memo: Subsistence farmers grow what their family eats. Anything extra might be shared with neighbours, but it's not the main goal.

questions.question: What is 'COMMERCIAL farming'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is commercial farming?
options: Farming crops or animals to sell for money
Farming to feed only your family
questions.expected: Farming crops or animals to sell for money
questions.memo: Commercial farming = farming for the market. Big maize farms, fruit farms and dairy farms in SA are mostly commercial.

questions.question: Which is an UNPROCESSED food?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is an unprocessed food?
options: A fresh apple straight from the tree
questions.expected: A fresh apple straight from the tree
questions.memo: Unprocessed = the way it came from nature. The apple is just an apple. Bread, beans in a tin, and crisps have all been changed.

questions.question: Which is a PROCESSED food?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a processed food?
questions.expected: Bread
questions.memo: Bread is processed — wheat is ground into flour, mixed with water and yeast, then baked. The carrot, egg and banana are still in their natural form.

questions.question: Put these in order — from farm to family table.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order, from farm to family table.
options: Wheat is grown on a farm
Wheat is taken to a mill and made into flour
The flour is baked into bread
The bread is bought and eaten at home
questions.expected: Wheat is grown on a farm,Wheat is taken to a mill and made into flour,The flour is baked into bread,The bread is bought and eaten at home
questions.memo: Farm → mill → bakery → shop → home. Each step is part of food processing. Most food you buy went through several steps.

questions.question: Which is one of South Africa's main CROPS?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is one of South Africa's main crops?
questions.expected: Maize
questions.memo: Maize (mielies) is South Africa's biggest grain crop. We grow huge amounts — much of it becomes pap, mealie meal, and animal feed.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa is a big producer of FRUIT for export.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa exports a lot of fruit to other countries.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. South African apples, grapes, oranges and avocados are sold around the world. The Western Cape and Limpopo grow large amounts of fruit.

questions.question: Which is 'LARGE stock'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is called large stock?
questions.expected: Cattle (cows)
questions.memo: Large stock = big animals like cattle. Small stock = sheep and goats. Poultry = chickens, ducks, geese.

questions.question: Why do people 'PROCESS' food (cook, dry, or grind it)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do people process food — cook it, dry it, grind it?
options: To make it safer, taste better, or last longer
To make it cost more for no reason
questions.expected: To make it safer, taste better, or last longer
questions.memo: Cooking kills germs. Drying makes food last longer. Grinding wheat into flour makes it usable. Processing is useful — though some processed food is over-processed.

questions.question: Lerato's family grows vegetables in their yard and eats them. This is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's family grows vegetables in their yard and eats them. What kind of farming is this?
options: A small kind of subsistence farming
questions.expected: A small kind of subsistence farming
questions.memo: Even a vegetable garden at home is subsistence farming — they grow it to eat, not to sell. Many South African families do this.

questions.question: True or false: People can also grow food in TOWNS and CITIES.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: people can also grow food in towns and cities.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Urban farming is growing — community gardens, rooftop gardens, backyard veggies. Food doesn't have to come from far away.

questions.question: Which is an example of 'poultry' farming?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is poultry farming?
options: Raising chickens for meat or eggs
questions.expected: Raising chickens for meat or eggs
questions.memo: Poultry = farm birds. Chicken is one of the most-eaten meats in SA. Poultry farming makes both meat and eggs.

questions.question: How are PROCESSED foods made? (Choose the BEST answer)
questions.ruby_prompt: How are processed foods made — what kinds of steps are used?
options: Cooking, drying, squeezing, cutting and mixing
questions.expected: Cooking, drying, squeezing, cutting and mixing
questions.memo: Processing covers MANY methods. Squeezing makes juice; drying makes biltong; cutting makes chips; mixing makes sauce; cooking makes most things edible.

questions.question: Why is it important to TAKE CARE of farm animals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to take care of farm animals?
options: Healthy animals are happier and produce better food (milk, eggs, meat)
Animals can take care of themselves alone
questions.expected: Healthy animals are happier and produce better food (milk, eggs, meat)
questions.memo: Animal care matters — for the animals AND the food. Sick or stressed animals produce poor food. Good farmers feed, shelter and treat their stock well.

questions.question: Tell me ONE food your family eats that started on a FARM.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one food your family eats that started on a farm.
questions.expected: Bread started as wheat on a farm
questions.memo: Good answers: maize/pap, bread, milk, eggs, chicken, apples, oranges, rice, beans, sugar — basically every food. All food traces back to farming.

questions.question: Which is a difference between SUBSISTENCE and COMMERCIAL farming?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a key difference between subsistence and commercial farming?
options: Subsistence feeds the family; commercial sells to make money
questions.expected: Subsistence feeds the family; commercial sells to make money
questions.memo: The PURPOSE is the difference. Same crops can be subsistence or commercial — depends on whether you eat it or sell it.

questions.question: Why does South Africa need BOTH subsistence and commercial farming?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does South Africa need both subsistence and commercial farming?
options: Commercial farms feed cities and earn money; subsistence farms feed families directly and protect against hunger
questions.expected: Commercial farms feed cities and earn money; subsistence farms feed families directly and protect against hunger
questions.memo: Big farms feed the country and export earn money. Small/subsistence farms protect families if shop prices rise or jobs are lost. Both matter.

SS.L4.GEO.T04.title: Water in South Africa
SS.L4.GEO.T04.description: Uses of water; salt and fresh water; the natural water cycle; how people store and access water; pollution and wastewater.
SS.L4.GEO.T04.recovery_strategy: Water moves in a cycle: sea → cloud → rain → river → sea. Salt water is in the sea; fresh water is what we drink. South Africa is a dry country, so we must use water carefully.

questions.question: Which kind of water can we DRINK?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which kind of water can we drink?
options: Dirty river water with no treatment
questions.expected: Fresh water
questions.memo: Only fresh water is safe to drink — and it usually needs to be cleaned first. Salt water makes you sicker the more you drink.

questions.question: Where is most of the world's SALT water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where is most of the world's salt water?
questions.expected: In the oceans and seas
questions.memo: Oceans hold about 97% of all water on Earth — but it's all salty. Only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is in ice.

questions.question: Which is a SOURCE of fresh water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a source of fresh water?
questions.expected: A river
questions.memo: Rivers carry fresh water from rain and mountains down to the sea. Other fresh water sources: lakes, streams, wetlands, underground water.

questions.question: What is the 'water cycle'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the water cycle?
options: The way water moves between sea, sky and land — over and over
questions.expected: The way water moves between sea, sky and land — over and over
questions.memo: Water heats up, rises as vapour, forms clouds, falls as rain, flows back to the sea, and starts again. The same water has been going around for billions of years.

questions.question: Put these in order — the water cycle.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in the right order — the natural water cycle.
options: The sun heats water in the sea, making it rise as vapour
Water vapour cools into clouds in the sky
Clouds release water as rain or snow
Water flows in rivers back to the sea
questions.expected: The sun heats water in the sea, making it rise as vapour,Water vapour cools into clouds in the sky,Clouds release water as rain or snow,Water flows in rivers back to the sea
questions.memo: Sun → vapour → clouds → rain → river → sea. The water you drink today may have been in the sea, then a cloud, last year.

questions.question: Which is a USE of water in our daily lives?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a daily use of water?
questions.expected: Drinking, washing, cooking and cleaning
questions.memo: Water is needed for so many daily things. Think of how many times you use a tap each day — drinking, brushing teeth, bath, washing hands.

questions.question: Which is another use of water (besides homes)?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where else (besides homes) is water used?
options: Farming, factories, mining and generating electricity
questions.expected: Farming, factories, mining and generating electricity
questions.memo: Farms use HUGE amounts of water for crops and animals. Factories use water to make things. Even electricity-making uses water. We share water with all of these.

questions.question: Why do people STORE water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do people store water?
options: So there is water available when it's not raining and when supplies run low
Because it tastes better when stored
questions.expected: So there is water available when it's not raining and when supplies run low
questions.memo: South Africa gets dry spells. Storing water in dams, tanks and buckets means we still have water when rains stop. Smart planning.

questions.question: What is a DAM?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a dam?
options: A wall built across a river to store a large amount of water
questions.expected: A wall built across a river to store a large amount of water
questions.memo: Dams hold back river water. The stored water then supplies cities, farms and factories. South Africa has many big dams.

questions.question: What is a BOREHOLE?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a borehole?
options: A deep hole drilled into the ground to bring up underground water
questions.expected: A deep hole drilled into the ground to bring up underground water
questions.memo: Underground water (groundwater) can be reached by drilling. Many South African farms and rural homes use boreholes for their water.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa is a country with PLENTY of water.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: South Africa has plenty of water — water is never scarce here.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: False. South Africa is a DRY country. Many areas get little rain, and droughts are common. Using water carefully matters a lot here.

questions.question: How does water get to most TAPS in homes?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does water get to most taps in homes?
options: From dams to purification plants to reservoirs through pipes to houses
From the sky directly into the tap
questions.expected: From dams to purification plants to reservoirs through pipes to houses
questions.memo: Dam → purified (cleaned) → reservoir → pipes → tap. Each step matters. The pipes carry CLEAN water all the way to your home.

questions.question: What is 'water pollution'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does water pollution mean?
options: Making water dirty so it's no longer safe to use
questions.expected: Making water dirty so it's no longer safe to use
questions.memo: Pollution is anything that makes water unsafe — chemicals, rubbish, sewage. Polluted water hurts people, animals and plants.

questions.question: Which is a way that EVERYDAY actions can pollute water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which everyday action can pollute water?
options: Throwing rubbish into rivers or stormwater drains
Washing your hands at a tap
questions.expected: Throwing rubbish into rivers or stormwater drains
questions.memo: Rubbish in stormwater drains flows straight to rivers and the sea. One plastic bag becomes a thousand small pieces. Small careless choices have big effects.

questions.question: What happens at a 'wastewater treatment plant'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What happens at a wastewater treatment plant?
options: Dirty water from homes is cleaned before being returned to rivers
questions.expected: Dirty water from homes is cleaned before being returned to rivers
questions.memo: Sewage and washing water go to a treatment plant. There it's cleaned in stages — rubbish removed, germs killed, then released clean. This protects rivers.

questions.question: Why might farms pollute water?
questions.ruby_prompt: How might farms pollute water?
options: Fertilisers and pesticides can wash into rivers when it rains
questions.expected: Fertilisers and pesticides can wash into rivers when it rains
questions.memo: Chemicals used on farms can wash off the soil into streams and rivers. This is one reason careful farming matters.

questions.question: True or false: We can USE water carefully so there's enough for everyone.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: if we use water carefully, there's more for everyone.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: True. Short showers, fixing leaks, turning off taps while brushing teeth — small habits add up. In a dry country every drop saved helps.

questions.question: Sipho lives where there is no tap. How might his family get water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's family doesn't have a tap in the house. How might they get their water?
options: From a shared community tap, a borehole, a river or a water truck
They have no water at all ever
questions.expected: From a shared community tap, a borehole, a river or a water truck
questions.memo: Many South Africans get water from shared taps, boreholes, rivers, or water trucks (where pipes haven't reached). Government works to bring pipes to more homes.

questions.question: Tell me ONE way YOU can use water more carefully at home.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one way you can use water more carefully at home.
questions.expected: I can turn off the tap while brushing my teeth
questions.memo: Good answers: short showers, full sink not running tap, fix leaks, water the garden in the evening, collect rainwater, reuse water. All real and useful.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about water?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which statement about water is true?
options: The amount of fresh water is limited; we must share and protect it
Salt water is the same as fresh water
questions.expected: The amount of fresh water is limited; we must share and protect it
questions.memo: Earth has the same water it always had. Fresh water is a small share of it. Use carefully + don't pollute = enough for all.
